overview: This atlas label groups changing parts of Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula and, in some snapshots, Borneo between 800 and 1279. It does not identify one kingdom or a population sharing one religion. Archaeology reveals ports, craft settlements and religious centres with different histories. Ancient Kedah comprised several settlements.

periods.title: Ports and sacred places
periods.summary: Kedah’s eighth- and ninth-century Bukit Choras temple belongs to an already connected maritime world.

periods.title: Merchants record their agreements
periods.summary: The Tamil inscription at Lobu Tua dates to 1088 and records merchant organization and taxation.

periods.title: Crafts continue across local changes
periods.summary: Research places Sungai Mas bead production within a long sixth- to thirteenth-century tradition; the atlas endpoint is not a common fall of these communities.

items.text: The 800 outline includes Barus and Kedah; the 1000 outline combines northern Sumatra and Borneo. Kedah returns in 1100 but lies south of the 1200 outline. These are atlas categories, not an empire’s expansion. Barus examples after 900 continue its local history beyond the drawn boundary.

Barus, on Sumatra’s western coast, exported camphor and appears in accounts from far beyond the island. Its archaeological goods include ceramics and glass connected with several Asian regions. A port’s importance could rest on forest products and shipping contacts, not simply on the size of a palace.

At Lobu Tua near Barus, excavators found an earthen fort with a surrounding ditch. Ceramics place the settlement broadly from the later ninth century to the end of the eleventh. A defended trading settlement needed shared space and collective effort as well as people arriving with cargo.

The Lobu Tua stone, now Museum Nasional object D.42, records a Tamil merchant guild in 1088. Its tax arrangements show traders acting together and writing down obligations. International commerce involved meetings and rules as well as adventurous voyages: somebody still had to sort out the bill.

Sungai Mas in Kedah made its own glass beads. A study tested 22 beads and raw-material samples rather than assuming every attractive bead came from India. Its results support local manufacture from the sixth through thirteenth centuries, a reminder that port communities were producers as well as customers.

Glassmakers’ choices affected both colour and whether a bead was transparent or opaque. Researchers examined major and trace elements associated with these properties at Sungai Mas. Small ornaments preserve evidence of considerable material knowledge; an ancient workshop was doing sophisticated things on a very tiny scale.

Barus finds include small round stone boxes with lids and an object compared with an eyebrow pencil. These may reveal personal grooming and cosmetics, although their exact uses remain uncertain. Archaeology sometimes gets surprisingly close to someone’s dressing table without recovering the person’s name.

sections.title: Building, learning and caring for places

items.text: At Bukit Choras, researchers announced two life-sized stucco statues in 2023, associated with a Buddhist temple dated to the eighth or ninth century. The surviving walls and stairs help reconstruct how people approached a sacred building. Similarities with objects in Sumatra and West Java reveal artistic connections, not a proven shared ruler.

A further Buddha found beside the north wall in 2024 was made of stucco, a mixture of lime, water and sand. This is a useful correction to the idea that ancient sculpture always meant carving solid rock: builders could shape a prepared mixture into a human-sized figure.

Bukit Choras studies also record two ancient water tanks, laterite-brick remains and iron nails. Water storage mattered to the site, but the available study summary does not establish the tanks’ exact dates or a toilet system. These are traces of infrastructure, not a complete account of household hygiene.

Researchers used contour maps, magnetism, electrical resistivity and ground-penetrating radar around Bukit Choras. Such methods look for buried structures before digging. Learning about the past can begin by measuring the ground rather than turning it into a giant hole.

The 2024 Bukit Choras statue was moved temporarily to a university laboratory for conservation and further study. Preserving an excavation is skilled work in its own right. A spectacular discovery needs careful handling before it can safely become something families learn from.

sections.title: A written witness and a nearby meal

items.text: A tiny bottle-green glass seal found at Lobu Tua in 1997 bears Arabic writing. Its second line can be represented in normalized modern letters as محمد, transliterated Muḥammad: the personal name Muhammad. Scholar Ludvik Kalus tentatively dated the object to the tenth or eleventh century. It was found outside a secure archaeological layer and was probably imported.

The seal measures only about 15 by 13 millimetres. Its letters were engraved backwards for making an impression; Kalus suggested it might also have served as a personal talisman. This individual object shows why the map’s Hindu-and-Buddhist label must not erase other beliefs or visitors.

Kota Cina near modern Medan lies outside these exact polygons, but offers a useful neighbouring comparison for northern Sumatran life. Layers dated broadly to the eleventh through thirteenth centuries contain wooden post sections and palm-fibre cord. Perishable building materials can survive when the ground preserves them, although these pieces do not reveal a whole family’s floor plan.

At the same nearby Kota Cina site, dense heaps of discarded shells are interpreted as food remains. Cockles and clams help put ordinary meals back into a story often dominated by imported luxuries. Dinner left evidence too, even when the plates, conversations and people have disappeared.

ending.text: There was no single collapse in 1279. Kedah settlements continued into the fourteenth century. Nearby Kota Cina was abandoned in the early 1300s; researchers suggest silting waterways may have impeded seagoing vessels. That is one local environmental explanation, not an ending for every port or community under this atlas label.
